name: DurableTimer
purpose: Workflow scoped sleep that persists across worker outages and fires after a logical delay so long delays do not hold process resources.
invariants: A fired timer MUST be recorded as an event so workflow replay reconstructs the same fire point.
Wall clock sleep calls inside a workflow are FORBIDDEN because they break determinism and do not survive outages.
A canceled timer SHALL NEVER fire; cancellation ALWAYS reaches the workflow before a fired event is recorded.
delay_s MUST be non negative; a negative delay CANNOT be scheduled and raises an argument error.
A single worker NEVER caps the number of concurrent durable timers at the process level because timers persist server side.
extension_contract: Add scheduling backends by implementing TimerService as an adapter over the orchestrator, and compose cross cutting policies (quota, fairness) by wrapping start with middleware registered on the worker.
consumption_example:
async def park_until(svc: TimerService, wf_id: str, seconds: float) -> None:
    timer = DurableTimer(workflow_id=wf_id, timer_id=f'wait-{seconds}', delay_s=seconds)
    await svc.start(timer)

sources.locator: docs.temporal.io/develop/python/timers Durability and Replay safety paragraphs
docs.temporal.io/workflows Durability and Event History section

why_essential: Long waits without holding a thread, and deterministic replay of delays, are orchestrator level primitives; each tool rolling its own asyncio sleep loses persistence and replay correctness.
alternatives_considered: asyncio.sleep inside workflow code which disappears on process restart
External cron style schedulers which cannot correlate to a workflow run id
